shipped_rows.title_o: Learning from video modeling examples: Effects of seeing the human model's face

blind_target.authors: Van Wermeskerken, M., & Van Gog, T.
blind_target.title: Seeing the instructor's face and gaze in demonstration video examples affects attention allocation but not learning.
blind_target.evidence_quote: This study replicated the face visible and face not visible conditions from our prior study (Van Wermeskerken & Van Gog, 2017) with adolescents in prevocational education, using the same molecule building task, to investigate whether or not seeing the model's face would affect learning outcomes in a younger population with a lower level of education.
blind_target.outcome_quote: With respect to the first aim, we replicated our previous findings in this adolescent population, by showing that their learning was not affected by the presence or absence of the model's face, even though they spent proportionally less time looking at the task area when the model's face was visible.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly state replication of their prior findings; the earlier Van Gog et al. paper is background in the replication chain, not the closest target.

luna_triage.reason: The paper explicitly states it aimed to replicate Van Wermeskerken and Van Gog (2017)'s finding in adolescents and reports on that test. The supplied row is Van Gog, Verveer, and Verveer (2014), a different earlier study in the chain; the source distinguishes the 2017 findings from the 2014 findings.

luna_triage.identity_quote: These findings, though, why we did not replicate the findings of Van Gog et al. (2014)
